summary: The US NTIA asked ICANN to propose how NTIA should end its oversight of the IANA functions, and ICANN created a coordination group to ask the affected communities for proposals. This informational document is the IETF's response to the request for proposals about the IANA protocol parameters registries.

eli5.summary: The US government used to oversee the keepers of the internet's lists of numbers and names. When it planned to hand that over, the IETF wrote its answer about how its lists should be kept.

questions: who runs the protocol parameter registries
who oversees the iana protocol parameters registries
subtitle: The IETF's formal answer on how the IANA protocol parameters registries should be run once the US government steps back.

tldr.problem: The US NTIA announced its intent to transition oversight of the IANA functions, and the ICG asked the protocol parameters, names and numbers communities for proposals.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF answers the ICG's questionnaire item by item, describing its existing arrangements with ICANN and proposing no new organizations or structures.
tldr.outcome: The response asks only for supplemental agreements, plus acknowledgments that the registries are in the public domain and that ICANN will help with any future change of operator.

today: RFC 7979 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the IETF's position as written for the 2014 and 2015 transition process.

sections.title: Why This Response Exists
sections.content:
In March of 2014, the US National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) announced its intent to transition oversight of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) functions and asked ICANN to establish a process for a transition proposal. The IANA Stewardship Transition Coordination Group (ICG) was formed and solicited proposals from the names, numbers and protocol parameters communities.

This RFC addresses only the protocol parameters registries. It quotes the ICG's questionnaire and gives the IETF's answers under the heading "IETF Response". The ICG charter and the full request for proposals are in appendices.
sections.eli5: Someone big asked each group to explain how its own list of numbers and names is looked after. This is the answer from the group that writes internet standards.

sections.title: What the IETF Uses IANA For
sections.content:
Many IETF protocols define parameter values that must be interpreted the same way by independent implementations. The specifications require globally available registries holding the values and pointers to documentation, and the IETF uses the IANA protocol parameters registries to hold them publicly. The response treats the .ARPA top level domain, which ICANN operates on behalf of the IAB, as part of these registries.

The IETF says it has no formal membership, so "the IETF" means anyone who participates. It describes points of interaction with other communities: special-use domain name registries coordinated with ICANN, the DNS protocol, root server requirements, and delegation of unicast IP address and AS number ranges to the RIRs. It says responsibility for each registry is carefully delineated, so there is no overlap in the sense of shared responsibility.
sections.eli5: Many internet rules need a shared list of agreed numbers so that every computer means the same thing. The IETF keeps those lists in public.

sections.title: Policy, Oversight and Disputes
sections.content:
Policy for the registries is stated in RFC 6220 and RFC 5226. All IETF policy begins as an Internet-Draft that anyone may submit, and it needs rough consensus and a Last Call before the IESG can approve it. Disputes are handled first through working groups and rough consensus, then through the appeals process in Section 6.5 of RFC 2026, which involves the Area Director, the IESG and the IAB, with a final appeal to the Internet Society Board of Trustees.

The IAB provides oversight of the registries and must approve the organization that acts as IANA operator. A memorandum of understanding (RFC 2860) between ICANN and the IETF has been in place since 2000, with an annual service level agreement supplement. An annual audit has been performed since 2014. The MoU lets either party terminate with six months notice.
sections.eli5: Anyone can suggest a rule, and it only passes if most people agree. If someone is unhappy, they can appeal to higher and higher groups.

sections.title: What the IETF Proposes
sections.content:
The proposal says no new organizations or structures are required, and that the current system has worked well without operational involvement from the NTIA. It asks for two things as part of the transition. First, all relevant parties should acknowledge that the protocol parameters registries are in the public domain. Second, ICANN should acknowledge that it will carry out its obligations under C.7.3 and I.61 of the NTIA contract to achieve a smooth transition to subsequent operators, should the need arise.

It also states six guiding principles, including that the function should be capably provided by the Internet technical community, that it needs openness, transparency and accountability, that changes should respect existing agreements ("evolution, not revolution"), and that the registries are a public service available to everyone.
sections.eli5: The IETF said the system already works, so no big changes are needed. It only wanted two promises written down: the lists belong to everyone, and the keeper will help if a new one is ever chosen.

sections.title: Consensus and Process
sections.content:
The IESG established the IANAPLAN working group to develop the response. The IESG approved it during the 18 December 2014 telechat, and the IAB approved a statement of support on 19 December 2014.

Two suggestions did not gain enough support: a stronger statement on what terms the IAOC should negotiate, and a suggestion that "iana.org" and associated marks be transferred to the IETF Trust. The working group chairs concluded that rough consensus existed although support was not unanimous. The RFC requests no IANA actions and seeks no parameter allocations or changes.
sections.eli5: Lots of people discussed the answer, and most agreed. A few ideas were left out because not enough people liked them.
